Pregnancy

Upper abdominal pain in pregnancy: possible causes and when to call

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An ache or burning feeling high in your abdomen can have several causes during pregnancy. Some respond to simple changes, while others need urgent care. Start with the severity, persistence and any accompanying symptoms rather than assuming it is only heartburn or the baby pressing under your ribs.

Start with how you feel, not a guess about the cause

Upper abdominal pain means discomfort above the navel or beneath the ribs. It may be burning, aching, cramping or sharp. Gas, constipation and reflux are common possibilities, but the location alone cannot tell you that pain is harmless. Pregnancy-related complications and problems in other organs can overlap.

Contact your maternity team promptly about new, persistent or worrying pain. Severe or sudden pain, collapse, heavy bleeding, chest pain or difficulty breathing needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for an antacid, a bowel movement or a change of position to prove what is happening when symptoms are severe. Early in pregnancy, local care may be through an early-pregnancy service or another urgent service.

Gas and slower digestion can cause pressure

Pregnancy hormones, including progesterone, can slow movement through the digestive system. Gas may feel like fullness, bloating or shifting cramps. Later, the enlarging uterus can add pressure around the stomach and bowel. Mild discomfort that settles after passing wind may fit this pattern, but that is not a test that excludes every other cause.

Smaller meals, eating at an unhurried pace and gentle activity if suitable may help. Notice whether particular foods repeatedly make you uncomfortable without cutting out entire food groups unnecessarily. If the pain becomes constant, you are vomiting repeatedly or you feel unwell, seek advice rather than continuing to treat it as trapped wind.

Constipation needs a practical plan, including a medicine review

Hormonal changes, changes in activity, too little fluid or fibre and some medicines can contribute to constipation. Iron supplements are one possible contributor. Hard or infrequent stools, straining and bloating may accompany it, but a new severe pain needs its own assessment.

Try gradually including fibre-containing foods such as fruit, vegetables, pulses and wholegrains, with adequate drinks and appropriate activity. Ask a pharmacist, midwife or clinician about a suitable laxative or stool-softening treatment if needed. Do not stop prescribed iron on your own: low iron also needs treatment, and the team can help adjust the preparation or manage its effects.

Heartburn can feel high in the abdomen or behind the breastbone

Hormonal changes can relax the valve between the stomach and oesophagus, allowing acid to move upward. Pressure from the growing uterus can contribute later. Burning after a meal, a sour taste, belching or bringing food back up may suggest reflux, but severe or persistent upper abdominal pain should not automatically be given that label.

The frequency of symptoms differs between studies and stages of pregnancy. A single percentage cannot tell you whether your own pain is expected. In particular, pain below the ribs with a headache, visual changes, vomiting or feeling very unwell needs urgent review even if it resembles indigestion.

Ways to ease mild reflux without restricting fluids

Smaller meals, staying upright after eating and leaving about three hours between food and bedtime may help. Raising your head and shoulders at night can be useful. Choose clothing that does not press uncomfortably on your abdomen and notice personal triggers such as rich foods, spicy dishes or caffeinated drinks.

Avoid alcohol and seek help to stop smoking during pregnancy. There is no blanket need to avoid drinking with meals; maintain hydration and spread drinks through the day if large amounts worsen fullness. Ask about pregnancy-appropriate antacids or alginates if simple measures are not enough. Acupuncture is not a substitute for assessing persistent pain or using a treatment plan recommended by your maternity team.

Stretching skin and muscle strain are different from internal pain

As the abdomen grows, skin can feel tight or itchy, and changes in posture or load can strain muscles. A comfortable position, supportive pillow or appropriately fitted maternity clothing may help some people. A support belt is an optional comfort measure to discuss if needed, not a way to diagnose or cure unexplained upper abdominal pain.

A plain moisturiser may soothe dry skin, but creams do not reliably prevent stretch marks, and rubbing lotion on the abdomen does not treat pain from an internal organ. Stop any support garment that causes discomfort. Persistent itching, especially without a rash or on the palms and soles, should be reported rather than assumed to be stretching skin.

Tightenings may be practice contractions, but timing matters

Braxton Hicks tightenings can be noticed during the second or third trimester. They tend to be irregular and do not progressively build like established labour. Changing position, resting or drinking may make some mild tightenings settle, but improvement or lack of improvement cannot reliably diagnose labour at home.

If you are under 37 weeks and have regular cramps or tightenings, contact the maternity unit immediately. Also call for leaking fluid, bleeding, reduced movements or concern that labour is starting. Do not wait for contractions to reach a particular interval when there are other warning signs. Your team will decide whether you need an examination or monitoring.

Early-pregnancy pain can need urgent assessment

Ectopic pregnancy occurs when a pregnancy develops outside the uterus. Pain may be felt low in the abdomen or on one side, but shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, faintness or feeling very unwell can also be warning signs. Vaginal bleeding may occur, and discomfort when passing urine or stool can be relevant. Severe pain or collapse is an emergency.

Miscarriage can also cause cramping and bleeding, while bleeding does not always mean a pregnancy is being lost. Back or pelvic pain, a feeling of rectal pressure or unusual discharge needs discussion in context. Neck pain alone is not a specific diagnostic sign. The gestational-age definition of miscarriage varies between countries; do not use a 20-week cutoff to decide whether symptoms deserve help.

Pain under the right ribs can be a pre-eclampsia symptom

Pre-eclampsia usually develops after 20 weeks and can also occur after birth. Warning symptoms include severe or persistent pain below the ribs, a severe headache, visual disturbances, vomiting or sudden swelling of the face or hands. A rapid change in swelling or weight can be worth reporting, but none of these signs can diagnose the condition alone.

High blood pressure may cause no noticeable symptoms, which is one reason antenatal checks matter. Seek immediate maternity advice for warning symptoms rather than waiting for the next appointment or assuming that a previously normal blood-pressure reading rules the condition out.

Risk factors help plan care, not decide who deserves assessment

A history of high blood pressure, kidney disease, diabetes or pre-eclampsia increases risk. Other factors can include a first pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, family history, higher body mass index and older maternal age. Guidance uses specific definitions when deciding on prevention, so a broad claim about being a teenager or over 35 is not a complete personal risk assessment.

Someone without recognised risk factors can still develop a serious complication. Ask your maternity team about your own prevention and monitoring plan; do not start aspirin or another preventive medicine from an online risk list. Equally, being labelled higher risk does not mean pain must be pre-eclampsia: the symptoms still need proper assessment.

Itching may point to a liver condition rather than stretching

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, or ICP, affects bile handling in the liver and can cause bile acids to build up. It is not simply a blocked bile duct or a bilirubin problem. Persistent itching without a rash is the usual clue, often worse at night and involving the palms or soles. Jaundice is less common; dark urine or pale stools also deserves medical advice.

Assessment includes bile-acid and liver blood tests. Itching can begin before results become abnormal, so persistent symptoms may require repeat testing. Frequency varies between populations; one in a thousand is not a universal estimate. Treatment for itching does not guarantee protection for the baby. Monitoring and birth timing depend on bile acids and the wider pregnancy picture.

Placental abruption can happen without obvious bleeding

Placental abruption means the placenta separates partly or completely from the uterine wall before birth. It can cause sudden abdominal or back pain, uterine tenderness or persistent, closely spaced contractions. It is a serious condition that needs emergency assessment.

Blood may remain concealed inside the uterus, so the absence of visible vaginal bleeding does not make it safe to wait. This is not the same as blood necessarily collecting inside the amniotic sac. Call for urgent help with severe pain or suspected abruption, and report reduced or changed fetal movements immediately. You do not need to prove the cause before seeking care.

Kidney and urinary problems remain possible in pregnancy

Kidney stones can cause severe pain in the side or back, sometimes with blood in the urine. A kidney infection may cause pain beneath the ribs or in the back, fever, chills, nausea or urinary symptoms. These problems are distinct from ordinary pressure on the bladder.

Burning when passing urine, unusual urgency, cloudy or bloody urine, fever or feeling unwell should be reported promptly during pregnancy. A kidney infection can become serious and requires treatment. Do not assume that drinking more water alone will manage fever and flank pain, or wait for every typical urinary symptom to appear.

Gallbladder, pancreatic and other digestive conditions can overlap

Gallstones may cause upper central or right-sided pain, sometimes with nausea or vomiting. Inflammation of the gallbladder is called cholecystitis; inflammation of the pancreas is pancreatitis. Pancreatitis can cause severe, persistent upper abdominal pain that spreads toward the back and needs urgent hospital care.

Appendicitis and peptic ulcer disease are other possibilities clinicians may consider. Food allergy or intolerance can also cause digestive symptoms, but they are not interchangeable diagnoses. Do not begin a broad exclusion diet or assume every pain after eating is an allergy. Sudden breathing difficulty or throat swelling after food is an emergency, while persistent abdominal symptoms need a clinical assessment.

Rib pain is not always an abdominal-organ problem

Costochondritis is inflammation around the cartilage joining ribs to the breastbone. It can produce chest-wall pain that changes with movement or pressure. Calling it a rib infection is misleading: infection is not the usual meaning of the diagnosis.

Do not diagnose a new chest pain by pressing on it yourself. Sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing blood or feeling faint needs urgent assessment because heart and lung problems can also occur during pregnancy. A clinician can help distinguish muscular or chest-wall discomfort from other causes and choose treatment suitable for pregnancy.

Give your maternity team a clear account of the symptoms

Explain how many weeks pregnant you are, where the pain is, when it began and whether it is constant or comes in waves. Mention fever or chills, vomiting, bleeding, fluid leakage, unusual discharge, painful urination, headache, visual changes or dizziness. Tell them about medicines, including iron and anything taken for reflux or pain.

Once you know your baby’s usual movement pattern, contact maternity care immediately if movements slow, stop or change; do not wait until morning. These examples are not an exhaustive checklist. If you feel something is wrong, call. Mild symptoms that settle may need simple care, but severe, persistent or associated symptoms deserve assessment before reassurance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Severe, persistent or associated symptoms need assessment before home treatment is used as reassurance.

ICP involves bile acids, pre-eclampsia can lack obvious early symptoms and placental abruption may have concealed bleeding.

How BeMama can help

Keep the local maternity contact number accessible and describe the timing, location and associated symptoms when calling.

When to seek help

Obstetric and local triage review remain pending. Use emergency services for severe illness and immediate maternity advice for warning symptoms or changed fetal movements.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pain location alone cannot distinguish a common discomfort from a complication.
  • Do not stop prescribed iron or restrict fluids to manage digestive symptoms.
  • Severe right-sided rib pain, headache or visual changes needs urgent review.
  • Bleeding may be absent in abruption, and persistent itching can need repeat blood tests.

Frequently asked questions

Is pain under the ribs always the baby pressing upward?

No. Pressure is one possibility, but severe or persistent pain can signal a condition needing urgent assessment.

Can I try an antacid first if the pain is severe?

Do not delay assessment of severe or concerning pain to test whether an antacid works.

Should I stop iron if it makes me constipated?

Do not stop prescribed iron on your own. Ask about managing constipation or changing the preparation while treating low iron.

Should I avoid water during meals to prevent reflux?

There is no blanket rule to do that. Stay hydrated and discuss a pattern that feels comfortable if large drinks worsen fullness.

Can a support belt or cream treat internal abdominal pain?

No. They may help comfort or dry skin in some circumstances but do not diagnose or treat an internal cause of pain.

How can I be sure tightenings are Braxton Hicks?

You cannot always tell at home. Regular tightenings before 37 weeks, fluid leakage, bleeding or changed movements need immediate maternity advice.

Does no bleeding rule out placental abruption?

No. Bleeding can be concealed. Severe pain or suspected abruption needs emergency assessment.

Why repeat tests if itching continues after a normal result?

In ICP, symptoms can start before bile acids or liver tests become abnormal. The maternity team can arrange repeat testing when needed.

Is costochondritis the same as an infected rib?

No. It describes inflammation at rib-cartilage joints. New chest pain still needs assessment rather than self-diagnosis.

Should I wait overnight if my baby moves less with the pain?

No. Contact maternity care immediately for reduced, stopped or changed movements.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
